what_its_for: Paliperidone palmitate is used to treat schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. It helps reduce symptoms such as hallucinations (hearing or seeing things that are not there), delusions (false beliefs), disorganized thinking, and unusual behavior. It works by balancing certain natural chemicals in the brain called dopamine and serotonin.
how_to_take: This medication is given as an injection by your doctor, nurse, or other healthcare provider. It is NOT a pill you take at home. Depending on which form you are prescribed, it may be given as a shot in your upper arm (deltoid muscle) or buttock (gluteal muscle). Your first two doses of Invega Sustenna are given one week apart to get the medication started in your body. After that, you will receive injections once a month, once every three months, or once every six months depending on which product your doctor prescribed. It is very important to keep all of your scheduled injection appointments.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. Common dosing schedules are: Invega Sustenna — given once a month; Invega Trinza — given once every 3 months (only after being stable on Invega Sustenna for at least 4 months); Invega Hafyera — given once every 6 months (only after being stable on Invega Trinza or Invega Sustenna for a period of time). Do not try to adjust your own dose. Always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: Because this medication is given by a healthcare provider, if you miss an appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Missing injections can cause your symptoms to return. Do not wait until your next scheduled appointment if you have already missed one — contact your healthcare team immediately so they can determine the best next step for you.
storage: You do not need to store this medication at home — your healthcare provider stores and gives it to you at each visit. If for any reason you are handling it, keep it at room temperature (between 59°F and 77°F or 15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from light and do not freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medication, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medication affects you. Avoid getting overheated or dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids in hot weather or when exercising. Tell your doctor before taking any other medications, including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal supplements, as some can interact with this medication. Avoid standing up too quickly from sitting or lying down, as this medicine may cause dizziness.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: uncontrollable movements of your face, tongue, or other body parts (could be a condition called tardive dyskinesia); high fever, stiff muscles, confusion, or sweating (signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); fainting, irregular heartbeat, or chest pain; trouble swallowing; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision; thoughts of harming yourself or others; a severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; or significant weight gain. Also call your doctor if you feel your symptoms are getting worse.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in your symptoms within the first few days to weeks after your injection, but it may take several weeks or even a few months to feel the full benefit of this medication. It is important to keep all of your injection appointments even if you are feeling better, because stopping treatment can cause your symptoms to return.
special_populations: Older adults: This medication should be used with caution in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, as it may increase the risk of stroke or death. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Babies born to mothers who took antipsychotic medications during the last trimester of pregnancy may experience withdrawal symptoms or movement problems. Breastfeeding: This medication may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney problems: Your dose may need to be adjusted or this medication may not be appropriate if you have moderate to severe kidney disease. Always tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions.
